title: Choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned Teletext. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Teletext
options.thesis: The archive as a broadcast service: every lost game is a numbered page, and remembering resolves its frame out of mosaic blocks.
options.viewport: Standard app shell: a black page header with the service name and a page number (P100), a left index of sections, and the main area as the archive index: numbered rows of lost games (P101 Pac-Man 99, 2021–2023) with mosaic still thumbnails, a search and category tabs as the four coloured fastext keys.
options.risk: Reads as retro novelty if the grid is not strict, and most 13+ visitors never saw real teletext.

raised.raise: Each page has one owner: the mosaic still or the index, never both fighting for the field.
Fit and difficulty ride one fixed ramp of 1–5 mosaic blocks, never as extra words.
States are marks: lost is a hollow block, remembering a flashing block, revived a solid block.

options.label: Contact Sheet
options.lineage: film contact sheets and the editor’s light table
options.thesis: Footage is the source: every game is a strip of frames, and Revive’s memory is grease-pencil notes on the contact sheet.
options.viewport: App shell with a dark rail; the archive as rows of film strips, three frames per game, name and years on the strip’s edge print; the open game shows its frames on a lit table with circled timestamps.
options.risk: The most expected reading of “footage”; close to what any run would ship for video.

options.label: Split-flap Concourse
options.thesis: Lost games as a departures board: cancelled rows in dim red, revivals flip to boarding.
options.viewport: App shell; the archive as a board of rows (game, platform, lost year, status) with flaps that cascade when a revival’s state changes.
options.case: Fuses cleanly and everyone knows the board; holds clarity, loses on how much of the gaming past it evokes.
options.risk: A table in costume if the flap motion is the only idea.

options.label: Character Roster
options.lineage: character goods catalogs and popularity rankings
options.thesis: Every lost game as a ranked portrait card with its born and lost dates; lost games print in grayscale, revivals in full colour.
options.viewport: App shell; the archive as a ranked roster grid of footage portraits, each with a name plate, years and its one-line note.
options.case: Strong product truth (grayscale until revived); holds clarity, loses identification with a gaming audience.
options.risk: Pastel softness fights the games’ own colours.

options.label: Monochrome Product
options.thesis: One neutral scale and one accent; every claim beside the footage frame that proves it.
options.viewport: App shell; the archive as a clean grid of footage frames with names and years, one violet Revive action.
options.case: Highest clarity, weakest identity: holds clarity only.

options.label: Factory Catalog Sleeve
options.thesis: Every game a catalog number on matte black.
options.case: Codes instead of names hurt clarity, and the reference is a design-nerd one.

options.label: Star Atlas
options.thesis: Lost games as stars sized by how much footage survives.
options.viewport: A sky chart of the archive.
options.case: A map is slower than a list for finding a game you already know.
options.kept: Importance on one fixed size ramp instead of labels.

options.label: Centre-rail Setting
options.thesis: The memory as an annotated edition.
options.viewport: Two text columns round a key rail.
options.case: Bookish; neither gamers nor the task live here.
options.risk: Reads as a library, not a game.
options.kept: States drawn as marks: hairline, filled, struck.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A dark game-library store, Steam-like, executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: Dark library shell with capsule thumbnails and a Revive button per game.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every game launcher by design.
